column2: Explainer "Infant mortality ... roughly 50% — half of children died before age 5"

column6: In industrial Manchester in the 1840s, roughly half of all children died before age 5.

column6: Q2: "perhaps 1-3 million slaves"; Explainer: "Estimates for Italy at its height range from about 1-1.5 million slaves (Scheidel) to 2-3 million (Brunt, Hopkins), the higher figures implying perhaps 35-40%..."

column2: Q1 expl "Caesar and Augustus made grain distribution free"
column5: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cura_annonae (Clodius gave free grain in 58 BC; later reduced to 150,000 recipients); Leges Clodiae
column6: The tribune Clodius made the distribution free in 58 BCE (frumentum publicum); Caesar and later Augustus kept it free but capped the number of recipients.

column2: Q5 "as price controls always do when the underlying monetary cause isn't addressed"
column5: The claim is conditional (controls without monetary correction); standard price-ceiling economics and the 301 CE Edict's failure support it. Wording is strong but not false
column6: none

column6: Q5: "the antoninianus, the larger coin that had by then displaced the denarius, held only 2-5% silver"; Explainer: "debased the silver coinage (the denarius and then the antoninianus that replaced it) from about 50%..."

column2: Explainer "Octavia Hill's model dwellings movement ... housing reformers like Charles Booth"
column5: Octavia Hill managed and improved existing houses (15 schemes, ~3,000 tenants by 1874; Homes of the London Poor, 1875); Booth was a social investigator (Life and Labour of the People, Wellcome Collection record)
column6: Philanthropic model dwellings companies, Octavia Hill's work managing and improving existing housing for poor tenants, the surveys of social investigator Charles Booth ... brought modest improvements

column6: Q1: "more than half of working-class children dying before age five (against about 20% of children of the higher classes)"; Q3: "about half of all children died before age five, roughly twice the rate in rural districts"; Explainer: "conditions in which more than half of working-class children died before age five"

column5: Lipsitz, The Possessive Investment in Whiteness / Civil Rights Commission, via crab.rutgers.edu/~glasker/FHADMIN.htm and Wikipedia "Institutional racism in the United States": $120 billion in federally backed housing 1934-62, less than 2% to nonwhites; no source for 36 million homes
column6: the federal government underwrote about $120 billion in new housing; by a widely cited estimate, less than 2% of it went to non-whites

column2: Q5 Matthew Effect: universal programs "avoid it"; applied to welfare "by Gunnar Myrdal"
column5: Deleeck 1978 "L'effet Mathieu" (Recherches sociologiques, sharepoint.uclouvain.be/sites/rsa/Articles/1978-IX-3_04.pdf): higher classes gain proportionally more from social policy; Korpi & Palme 1998 "paradox of redistribution" (LIS WP 174). Universal programs are more prone to the effect, not immune
column6: Question now asks why universal programs, though prone to the effect, prove more durable; answer defines the effect as middle-class capture, presents means-tested erosion as the political price of targeting, adds Korpi-Palme paradox; explanation credits Deleeck (late 1970s) instead of Myrdal

column2: Q4 "the LHC ... operates on the same basic principle but at energies billions of times greater"
column5: LHC is a synchrotron (fixed orbit, ramped fields), not a fixed-field spiral cyclotron. Also the energy ratio is ~10^8 vs the 80 keV 1931 cyclotron (6.8 TeV LHC beam), not billions
column6: a synchrotron 27 km in circumference, still uses magnets to steer particles around a ring and boosts them on each pass, but it keeps them on a fixed orbit rather than a spiral and reaches energies many orders of magnitude greater

column2: Explainer "Boyle established chemistry"
column5: Overstatement; the same Explainer says chemistry needed further revolutions in the 18th century (Lavoisier). Boyle's Sceptical Chymist (1661) pushed chemistry toward experiment

column6: Universities were not the only setting -- much scientific work also happened in royal courts, informal academies, and scientific societies, though many leading figures studied or taught at universities.

column2: Q2 "Newton (who thought kinetic energy was proportional to velocity)" and "kinetic energy = ?mv2"
column5: vis viva controversy: Newtonians/Cartesians measured a body's "force" by quantity of motion mv; Leibniz by vis viva mv^2 (SEP du Châtelet entry). Kinetic energy is (1/2)mv^2; "?" was an encoding glitch
column6: argued against the Newtonian view that the 'force' of a moving body is measured by its quantity of motion, mv, in favor of Leibniz's vis viva, mv squared -- the quantity behind what we now call kinetic energy, (1/2)mv^2

column2: Core "Franklin's X-ray crystallography revealed DNA's structure"
column5: Watson and Crick built the model; Franklin's data (Photo 51) was key evidence, as the file's own Q0 and Explainer say
column6: provided key evidence for DNA's structure

column2: Q3 federal university research funding "essentially zero before 1940"
column5: Hatch Act of 1887 (https://www.lsuagcenter.com/portals/communications/publications/agmag/archive/2012/spring/history-of-the-hatch-act-of-1887): federal funds to land-grant experiment stations from 1887, raised by the Adams (1906), Purnell (1925) and Bankhead-Jones (1935) Acts
column6: surged from modest sums before 1940, mostly for agricultural research at land-grant colleges' experiment stations, to hundreds of millions annually by 1950
